description: Pelvic tilt guide: gently flatten and release your lower back to warm up the lower abs and ease stiffness. Covers mistakes plus easier and harder versions.
intro: A pelvic tilt is a small rocking movement of the pelvis while you lie on your back. It wakes up the lower abdominals and loosens the lower back. In a pelvic floor routine it is a gentle warm-up that helps you find your pelvis before you add Kegels.
feel: You should feel your lower back press lightly into the floor, a mild effort in the lower belly, then a soft release. You should not feel your glutes do all the work, your breath stop or any push down into the pelvis. Rest a hand on your lower belly: it should firm gently as you tilt and soften as you release.

mistakes.wrong: Lifting your hips off the floor like a bridge
mistakes.right: Keep your tailbone down. The pelvis rocks, it does not rise.

mistakes.wrong: Squeezing the glutes hard to move
mistakes.right: Let the lower abs lead and keep your buttocks relaxed.
Exhale as you flatten your back and inhale as you release. One slow breath per rep is a good pace.

easier: Make the movement smaller, or do the tilt standing with your back against a wall.
harder: Hold the flattened position for three to five seconds, or add a gentle Kegel as you flatten and fully relax the pelvic floor as you release.
who: Good for people with a stiff lower back, desk workers, older adults, and anyone easing back into exercise after childbirth once a health professional has cleared them.
skip: If you are pregnant beyond the first trimester, ask your midwife or doctor about lying on your back; you can tilt on hands and knees or standing instead. See a doctor or pelvic floor physiotherapist first after recent pelvic or abdominal surgery or with new back pain. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: Do pelvic tilts strengthen the pelvic floor?
faq.a: Not much on their own. They mainly work the lower abs and improve pelvic awareness, which can make Kegels easier to find and control.

faq.q: Are pelvic tilts safe after giving birth?
faq.a: They are often one of the first moves offered after birth. Get clearance from your doctor or midwife first, especially after a C-section.
